objectives.statement: Identify psql as PostgreSQL's terminal-based front end for issuing queries and viewing results.
Explain the purpose of pg_dump as a utility for exporting a PostgreSQL database.
Distinguish COPY FROM from COPY TO when moving data between a table and a file.
Identify the PostgreSQL client and server sides involved in file access by COPY and by \copy.
Identify pg_restore as the utility for restoring non-plain-text archives created by pg_dump.
Distinguish plain-text SQL dumps from archive formats in the PostgreSQL dump workflow.
Explain how the psql \copy meta-command routes files through the client connection.
Identify text, CSV, and binary as the data formats supported by COPY and the default format.
Explain how psql reads commands from a file with the -f option.
Explain how pg_dump provides consistent exports while concurrent database activity continues.
Distinguish the custom and directory archive formats by their restoration and parallelism capabilities.
Explain how pg_restore can select or reorder archive items before restoration.
Distinguish server-side file access by COPY from client-side file access by \copy.
Explain how COPY with STDIN or STDOUT transfers data through the client connection.
Identify the portability and type-specificity trade-offs of COPY binary format.
Identify the privileges needed for pg_dump to read the objects being exported.
Recognize the security risk that restoring a dump executes code chosen by source superusers.
Identify the security implications of COPY PROGRAM and the server roles that permit server-file or program access.
Apply the PostgreSQL procedure for restoring a plain SQL dump, including database creation and psql invocation.
Use pg_restore list and use-list options to inspect and constrain archive restoration order.
